title: Judith (Judith 8–13)
hook: a widow rebukes the elders for testing God and saves her city

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tobias and Sara began their marriage on their knees, and Raguel filled in the grave. Your line was pray together first. Who did you stop with, before the day began? Day four hundred thirty-nine.

A small hill town called Bethulia is under siege. A huge army under the general Holofernes has surrounded it and cut off the springs. The cisterns are running dry. Children are fainting in the streets. The people gather around the town's leaders and shout: surrender. Better to be slaves and alive than to watch our children die of thirst. So the chief elder, Ozias, makes a deal with them. Hold out five more days. If God hasn't helped us by then, we'll open the gates. It sounds reasonable. It sounds like faith, even. And a widow in the town hears about it.
screen: `A HILL TOWN UNDER SIEGE.` → `THE SPRINGS CUT OFF.` → `FIVE MORE DAYS, THEN SURRENDER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Judith, which simply means a Jewish woman, a woman of Judea. Her husband had died of sunstroke at the barley harvest, and for over three years she'd lived as a widow, fasting and praying, wealthy and widely respected; nobody, the book says, spoke an ill word of her. She sends for the elders, and she doesn't soften it. Who are you, she asks, to put God to the test? You've set a deadline for the mercy of the Lord, and appointed him a day of your own choosing. God isn't a man, to be threatened or bargained with. If he wants to save us, he can, in his own time. Then she tells them she has a plan, and that they're not to ask what it is. She prays, takes off her widow's clothes, dresses in her finest, and walks out of the town gate with her maid, straight into the enemy camp. She tells Holofernes she's come to help him win. He is charmed. On the fourth night he throws a banquet, drinks more than he ever has, and falls asleep, and Judith, alone in the tent, takes his own sword and kills him. She carries his head back to the town in her food bag, and the army, leaderless, breaks and runs. It's a hard, bloody story, and the book doesn't look away. It also doesn't read like a chronicle: it opens with Nabuchodonosor ruling the Assyrians from Nineveh, which history doesn't match, so many scholars, Catholic ones among them, read it as a story told to teach. What it teaches is clear: when the leaders gave up, a widow didn't.
screen: `JUDITH: A WOMAN OF JUDEA.` · `YOU SET A DEADLINE FOR GOD'S MERCY.` · `INTO THE ENEMY CAMP.` · `A STORY TOLD TO TEACH.` · then, large: `WHEN THE LEADERS GAVE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find where you might need to speak up. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you belong where the people in charge have quietly given up. A team at work, a parish committee, a family, a school, a town. Maybe they've set a deadline for hope. Maybe they've decided nothing can change. Don't plan anything dramatic. Just ask what one respectful, honest sentence you could say to them would be, the way Judith called the elders and told them the truth. If you pray, you can ask for her courage. The bell holds the time.
Judith. The widow of Bethulia who rebuked the elders for putting God on a deadline, and then went out and saved her city. Today's word.
Your line: a widow saved the city. Today, say the honest sentence you found, kindly, to someone who has given up. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 439 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN THE HAND OF GOD.`

howItsDone: Catholics hear Judith in the Liturgy of the Hours and at Mass, and the Church's liturgy applies the praise given to Judith, blessed above all women, to the Virgin Mary.

original.note: Hebrew: Judith, a Jewish woman, a woman of Judea. the book itself survives in Greek and Latin.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gory tale of a woman with a sword.
what it means: a widow refuses to let her town's leaders put God on a deadline, and acts with faith when they've given up.
what a scholar hears: Yehudit, simply a Jewish woman; deliberate anachronisms like an Assyrian Nabuchodonosor suggest a story told to teach; the Church sings Judith's praise of Mary.

notes: All of Judith is paraphrased; the Douay (Vulgate) and Greek differ in verse numbering and detail.
Judith's husband Manasses died of sunstroke at barley harvest (8:2–3); widowhood 'three years and six months' in Vulgate, 'three years and four months' in Greek: 'over three years' used. Confirm.
Holofernes killed on the fourth day/night (Greek 12:10); confirm the detail as told.

Anachronism statement (Nebuchadnezzar as king of Assyria in Nineveh): standard in Catholic scholarship (e.g. introductions in the NAB, Jerusalem Bible). Confirm wording 'many scholars, Catholic ones among them'.
Liturgical use of Judith 13:18/13:23 and 15:9–10 for Mary (e.g. 'Tu gloria Ierusalem'): confirm.
The violence is described plainly but without detail; confirm tone is acceptable for the app.
